title: Seven Rounds, Three Hundred Crunches, One Cursed Wish
subtitle: This week: a typhoon-proof boxing session, Wile E. Coyote's boulder problem, a sci-fi swing-and-miss called Hope, and the wish in Obsession you can't take back
excerpt: A storm didn't stop training, it just meant kicks and spinning elbows got added to the mitts. That same logic of not getting to opt out once things have started runs through a Wile E. Coyote legal drama, a disappointing Korean sci-fi swing, and a cursed-wish horror film that plays like a fight you're not allowed to stop.
intro_md:
Typhoon signal was up all week, the kind where the sensible move is to stay home, but staying in only makes you feel like you skipped the week entirely, so we went in anyway. Turns out the stand-in coach had a very different idea of what 'just get one session in' meant. Five rounds, two minutes each, thirty seconds rest, mitts only, standard enough. Then round six he decided we needed kicks in the mix, and it turns out I have never in my life thrown a kick that resembled anything other than a man losing an argument with his own leg. Humbling in the way only genuinely being bad at something new can be. By round seven he was teaching spinning elbows off a combination that had me rotating the wrong direction every single time, which was apparently the universal signal that mitts were done for the day. Seven rounds total, in the end. Three hundred ab crunches in various flavours followed, because the man is old school to his bones and will get his three hundred crunches out of you whether or not you think crunches are an efficient way to build a core, which I don't, for the record.

That's the kind of week it's been. Showing up despite the weather, doing whatever the coach in front of you decides the session actually is, and finding out how much worse you are at kicking than you assumed. Horror and endurance both run on that same logic, which is roughly the thread underneath everything below, from a cursed wish you can't take back once it's cast to a coyote who has made peace with pushing his particular boulder forever.

film_blurbs.title: Coyote vs. Acme (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
I didn't expect the best Albuquerque-set legal drama I've seen in years to also be a Wile E. Coyote movie, but here we are. The premise is a class-action suit against the ACME corporation for decades of faulty products, and it plays it entirely straight, which is what makes it so funny.

Underneath the joke there's something that landed harder than I expected. Coyote never actually catches the Roadrunner and never really wants to, not deep down. He just wants the process. There's something in that which felt oddly familiar by the end of this particular week, showing up for the grind and quietly enjoying it despite yourself.

There's a genuine warmth in how the film treats its central duo, coyote and rock, more or less as friends stuck in the same Sisyphean bit together. I laughed more than I expected and got weirdly choked up near the end, which is not a sentence I thought I'd write about a movie with an anvil gag in it.

film_blurbs.title: Hope (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
This is the one I have more conflicted feelings about. I went in hoping for something with the gut-punch clarity of The Wailing, that particular strain of Korean genre film where the dread and the sci-fi turn both land because the groundwork gets laid early. Hope has the ingredients. Genuinely sharp Korean genre craft, a sci-fi tease running under the surface, CGI that's better than it has any right to be.

What it doesn't have is the patience to earn any of it. The film opens obscure, which is fine, then throws a genuinely distinct alien design at you that leaves you wanting a lot more of it, in a way that reads like the first chapter of a trilogy rather than a complete film on its own. That could have been brilliant. Instead the time that should have gone into building out the alien side of the story goes into extended comedic detours, including one exposition dump involving a finger up someone's backside that added precisely nothing to the film.

It's an absurdist swing at the standard blockbuster formula, and I clock what it's going for. I just wish the swing had a plot attached to it, instead of an alien Swiss cheese full of holes you keep hoping will fill back in. By the end I was hoping, beyond hope, that Michael Fassbender would show up and rescue the thing. Turns out he'd been there the whole film, playing the CGI alien. My disappointment could not be measured with instruments currently available to science.

film_blurbs.title: The Dog Stars (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
Adapted from Peter Heller's novel, this is a quiet, bruised film about a man flying a small plane over a depopulated world, keeping a routine going because the routine is the only thing standing between him and giving up entirely. There's a rhythm to his day, fuel checks, patrol laps, small rituals, that reminded me a lot of the boring mechanical parts of a training week nobody puts in the trailer. The wraps, the same warm-up drills, the walk to the gym in weather you'd rather not walk in.

The film is more interested in endurance as a psychological act than a physical one, which fits. Most of what gets you through mile ten of a long run, or the last thirty seconds of a round you're losing, isn't strength. It's just refusing to let the day's structure collapse.

film_blurbs.title: The Whisper Man (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
This one sits closer to crime thriller than horror, but it's got a creeping, patient dread running under the surface that I found harder to shake than plenty of films that lean harder into scares. A father relocates with his son after a loss, into a town with its own history of missing children, and the film takes its time letting that history seep back in.

It's a slow-burn watch, more about dread accumulating than jump scares landing, and I mean that as a compliment given how much of the genre right now goes the opposite way. Worth putting on if you want something that unsettles you at the pace of a long jog rather than a sprint.

horror_deepdive.title: The Wish You Can't Take Back
horror_deepdive.body_md:
Curry Barker's [feature directorial debut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obsession_(2025_film)) is a cursed-wish horror film, one of the oldest engines in the genre. Somebody wants something badly enough to make a bargain for it, and the bargain turns out to have teeth. What makes Barker's version land is how contemporary the mechanism feels. This isn't a monkey's paw or a witch in the woods. [Obsession gives chilling modern relevance to a classic tale of a wish gone wrong](https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/reviews/obsession-curry-barker-plays-twisted-ideas-manosphere-violent-make-wish-horror), and the wish itself comes wrapped in the language of an app or a subscription service.

The detail that stuck with me is the customer service call. At some point [Bear calls One Wish Willow customer service and learns the wish only ends if he or Nikki dies](https://movies.fandom.com/wiki/Obsession_(2025)). There is a support line for this. There is presumably a hold queue. And the answer, when it finally comes, is that the only two exits are somebody's death. Not a refund, not a form to fill out. What makes it worse is what Bear actually wants out of that call. He isn't asking to undo the spell entirely. He wants Nikki still obsessed with him, just without the part where it curses everyone involved. He wants the outcome kept and the mechanism removed. Read into that whatever you want about a certain flavour of guy who thinks the problem with coercion is the paperwork.

[Bear wants this to end, but he can't take his wish back](https://nofilmschool.com/obsession-ending-explained), and that single fact turns the second half of the film into a countdown with exactly one door out. I kept thinking about that phone call in relation to the mental furniture of a fight, or even a session like the one this week. Before it starts there's a version of you weighing whether to bother, deciding if it's worth it in this weather, with this coach, on this little sleep. That version of you has options. Once the mitts are up and round one starts, that guy is gone. You don't get a vote on whether round six turns into kicks or round seven turns into spinning elbows you cannot land in either direction. There's no line you call to renegotiate the terms. You made the wish the day you walked in through the door, and now the only way out is when the coach says it's over, not when your legs do.

That's the actual weight behind the phrase going the distance, and why it gets thrown around more casually than the reality deserves. Distance isn't a number of rounds. It's the acceptance, made in advance, that quitting is not something you get to reach for once things start going worse than planned. What Obsession understands, and what makes it stick with you longer than a straightforward monster movie, is that the horror isn't a thing chasing you. It's a rule you agreed to before you understood what agreeing to it meant.

closing_md: Hands are still faintly stinging from those spinning elbows I never once landed correctly, and there's a run pencilled in for tomorrow that the weather may or may not allow. No customer service line for that either. See you next week.
